Stone Fox
STOHN FOKS
noun (Boomer slang)
Fox, an attractive young woman, is African-American slang from the early twentieth century, mainstream by the 1960s (foxy, 1960s–70s; Jimi Hendrix’s "Foxy Lady," 1967). The intensifier stone — "completely, utterly," as in stone cold, stone crazy, stone deaf — is old English, revived in 1960s Black and hippie slang. Stone fox, a strikingly beautiful woman, was common in the late 1960s and 1970s.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A stone fox is a strikingly beautiful woman — the highest compliment a 1970s man could pay a woman’s looks. The grandparents’ version of today’s baddie. The Christian observation: Scripture does not pretend beauty is unimportant. It calls Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Abigail, and Esther fair, and the Song of Solomon has a husband say to his bride, "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Son 4:7). In marriage, a man’s delight in his wife’s beauty is holy. But the slang ranks women by their looks and puts them on display for any man’s appraisal, and Scripture refuses that ranking. "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30). The adornment God values is "the hidden man of the heart ... even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). And Scripture speaks directly to the man doing the looking. "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids" (Pro 6:25). Our Lord went further: "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mat 5:28). Job’s resolution is the godly man’s: "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" (Job 31:1). A grandfather who calls Grandma a stone fox after fifty years of marriage is using the word as the Song does. A young man who calls a stranger one is being asked by Scripture where his eyes are going.

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1960s–70s slang (fox, an attractive woman, + intensifier stone) for a strikingly beautiful woman — a beauty Scripture celebrates within marriage (Son 4:7) but ranks below the fear of the LORD (Pro 31:30), and guards from the lustful eye (Mat 5:28).

STONE FOX, n. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s) A very attractive woman. From fox (an attractive woman; AAVE, early 20th c.) + stone (completely, utterly). Compare foxy, foxy lady.

Webster (1828) — FOX, noun 1. An animal of the genus Canis, with a straight tail, yellowish or straw-colored hair, and erect ears. This animal burrows in the earth, is remarkable for his cunning, and preys on lambs, geese, hens or other small animals. 2. A sly, cunning fellow. 3. In seaman’s language, a seizing made by twisting several rope-yarns together.

Decode for families: the 1970s stone fox is the 2020s baddie; the same counsel applies to both.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Pro 6:25 — "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids."

Mat 5:28 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."

Job 31:1 — "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?"

Son 4:7 — "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee."

Modern Corruption

Stone fox ranks women by their looks and invites every man’s appraisal; Scripture celebrates beauty within marriage, ranks the fear of the LORD above it, and binds the eyes of men by covenant.

expand to see more

Notice the animal in the word. A fox is a prize to be hunted, admired for its sleekness, and chased. The slang made women quarry and men hunters, and the sexual revolution that ran alongside it made the hunt respectable. Many marriages of that generation were wrecked by men who never stopped looking for the next stone fox. Proverbs 6 is a long warning against exactly that, and it ends at the grave.

Scripture’s alternative is not to pretend beauty does not exist; it is to put beauty in its place. In marriage, a husband should delight in his wife — the Song of Solomon is in the Bible on purpose. Outside of it, a man makes a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). And everywhere, the woman most worth admiring is the one who fears the LORD (Pro 31:30), whose beauty does not fade with the years because it was never only skin.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English fox + early-20th-c. AAVE fox (an attractive woman) + intensifier stone (utterly) → late-1960s–70s stone fox.

expand to see more

Old English fox — the animal; figuratively a crafty person (Luk 13:32, "that fox")

Early 20th c. AAVE: fox — an attractive young woman

1960s–70s: foxy; "Foxy Lady" (Hendrix, 1967)

Intensifier stone — completely (stone dead, stone cold), revived in 1960s slang

Late 1960s–70s: stone fox
